items.definition: A speaking activity in which learners act out a short situation, such as a job interview or a customer complaint, using invented roles and dialogue.
items.example: In our one-to-one lesson I asked my student to do a role-play in which she handled a difficult phone call.
items.note: Usually written with a hyphen as a noun: role-play. The version without a hyphen is also accepted.

items.definition: A task that requires learners to move, speak or produce something during the lesson, rather than only listening or writing.
collocations: an interactive activity for the whole class
items.example: I planned an interactive activity so that my adult learner would practise speaking instead of taking notes for forty minutes.
items.note: In British English 'interactive' is sometimes used informally for any task that involves students talking.

items.definition: A short session in which a group generates as many ideas as possible about a topic, usually before evaluating them.
items.example: We spent ten minutes brainstorming topics for a presentation before narrowing the list down to three.
items.note: It can be a count noun: a brainstorm. In British English 'brainstorm' is also a verb meaning to discuss ideas informally.

items.definition: To express the main points of a text or a talk in a shorter form, without losing the essential meaning.
items.example: Please summarise the article in no more than three sentences before our next meeting.
items.note: The noun is 'summary'. 'A summarization' is not used in standard English.

items.definition: To examine information carefully in order to identify patterns, causes or meaning, and to draw conclusions from it.
collocations: a close analysis of the figures
items.example: The students analysed a set of customer survey results and presented their findings to the group.
items.note: British English spelling -ise; American English writes analyze. The noun is 'analysis'.

items.definition: To state exactly what a word or idea means, or to explain the boundaries of a concept so that others can use it correctly.
items.example: Before the role-play I defined three key terms that my learner had never met in written English.
items.note: Usually followed by a noun: define a concept. A 'definition' is the written form of the same idea.

items.definition: To reach a final decision or summary after examining evidence, or to bring a lesson or a discussion to a close.
items.example: We concluded the session by reviewing the new vocabulary and agreeing on three tasks for the week.
items.note: Use 'conclude that...' for findings and 'conclude the lesson' for finishing. The noun is 'conclusion'.

items.definition: To make something clear to someone by describing the reasons, the process or the steps involved, in a way they can follow.
items.example: Could you explain the difference between 'faster' and 'the fastest' in a sentence I would say at work?
items.note: More natural than 'make an explanation'. For something complex, 'break it down' is a common informal alternative.

items.definition: To make an idea, instruction or misunderstanding easier to understand, often by asking questions or adding detail.
items.example: I asked my tutor to clarify the wording of the assignment, and she sent me a clearer version.
items.note: The noun is 'clarification'. The word is slightly formal but very common in academic and workplace settings.

items.definition: To express the same idea in different words, which shows that you have understood the meaning rather than only memorised the wording.
items.example: In the speaking card, my student had to paraphrase the article without reusing the original vocabulary.
items.note: In examinations, copying the wording of the question is not paraphrasing.

items.definition: To participate in an activity, a discussion or an event, usually as a free choice rather than an obligation.
collocations: invite someone to take part in
items.example: Not everyone wants to take part in front of the group, so I gave my student a written option.
items.note: More formal than 'join in'. It is normally followed by a noun, not a gerund: take part in the event.

items.definition: To give ideas, effort or information that helps to achieve a shared result or to complete a piece of work.
items.example: Each member of the group contributed to the final presentation, but I asked one person to pull it all together.
items.note: Never followed by an object: 'contribute to the report' is right, 'contribute the report' is wrong.

items.definition: Practice in which two learners work together on a task for a few minutes before the class reconvenes.
items.example: We did pair work on the pronunciation of the past tense for about eight minutes.
items.note: Also used as a verb, to pair up. The teacher usually decides who works with whom.

items.definition: An activity in which three or more learners cooperate to complete a shared task and then present the result to the class.
items.example: Group work gave my learner the chance to use English with colleagues rather than only with me.
items.note: The alternative spelling 'groupwork' is common in course handbooks. Teachers often worry about uneven participation.

items.definition: Comments and suggestions that learners give to each other on their work, rather than feedback given by the teacher.
items.example: I introduced peer feedback so that my student would learn to comment politely on someone else's writing.
items.note: A 'peer' is a person of the same status. 'Peer review' is the academic version of the same idea.

items.definition: A written outline of what a teacher intends to do in a lesson, including aims, stages, materials and timing.
items.example: I shared my lesson plan before the session so that my learner could see how the hour would run.
items.note: In state education, 'lesson planning' usually names the work and 'a lesson plan' the document itself.

items.definition: A clear statement of what a learner should be able to do by the end of a lesson or course, written as an observable action.
items.example: The learning objective for today was to use the present perfect to talk about unfinished business.
items.note: Often confused with 'aim'. An objective describes the learner's performance, not the teacher's intention.

items.definition: The knowledge or skill a learner has actually gained by the end of a course, as opposed to what was planned in advance.
items.example: The course description lists the learning outcomes, but the real test is whether my learner can use phrasal verbs confidently.
items.note: Compare with 'learning objective': the objective is planned, the outcome is what was actually achieved.

items.definition: A detailed scoring guide that sets out the criteria for an assignment and the level of performance expected at each grade.
items.example: The rubric told me exactly what the examiner expected, so I could prepare my learner accordingly.
items.note: Common in US and international English. In British schools 'marking criteria' is the more usual phrase.

items.definition: The record of who is present at a lesson or event, and the act of being there regularly.
items.example: Attendance dropped before the exam because several learners had work commitments.
items.note: It is also the noun for the number of people present: attendance was low.

items.definition: The latest time by which a piece of work must be completed and submitted.
items.example: My learner works night shifts, so a flexible deadline is much more realistic than a fixed one.
items.note: As a verb it takes a direct object: deadline the report. 'Dead line' as two words is not standard.

items.definition: Extra time given to complete a task, or an additional task that goes beyond the basic requirements for faster learners.
items.example: The teacher offered an extension for anyone who finished the writing task early.
items.note: In technology an 'extension' is a browser add-on, so check the context.

items.definition: To give a piece of written or digital work to a teacher for marking, usually at the end of a lesson or by a deadline.
items.example: Could you hand in the writing task by Friday so that I can mark it before our next lesson?
items.note: Standard in British English. American English usually prefers 'turn in'.

items.definition: To return work to a learner after it has been marked or corrected.
items.example: I hand back the corrected essays with comments so that my learner can revise them independently.
items.note: Usually takes an object plus 'to somebody': hand the essays back to her.

items.definition: To check on the progress of something that has already been started, especially after an earlier action or conversation.
items.example: I follow up on the writing task by email, because some learners need a nudge before the deadline.
items.note: Written as three words in the verb form; the noun is 'a follow-up' with a hyphen.

items.definition: To arrange the equipment, furniture or digital system so that something can be used or carried out.
items.example: It takes me five minutes to set up the video call before each one-to-one lesson.
items.note: In American English this is also the usual way of saying 'create an account'.

items.definition: To stay at the same level as other people or as the demands of a course, in terms of work or new information.
items.example: When my learner missed two lessons she found it difficult to keep up with the rest of the group.
items.note: Often used negatively: I cannot keep up. 'Keep up to date with' has a slightly different meaning.

items.definition: To get the information or skills you missed so that you are level with the rest of the group again.
items.example: I record the lesson so that she can catch up on the grammar she missed while she was travelling.
items.note: Almost always followed by 'on'. 'Catch up' on its own means to reach the same point as others.

items.definition: To make a discussion or a session easier and more productive by guiding the participants rather than dominating it.
items.example: My role in this class is to facilitate the conversation, not to correct every small mistake.
items.note: Formally written with a -c-. In modern methodology it is often contrasted with 'teach'.

items.definition: To support a learner step by step with prompts, examples and temporary help that is gradually removed as the learner becomes independent.
items.example: I scaffold the speaking task with sentence frames, then remove them in the final part of the lesson.
items.note: A metaphor borrowed from construction. The noun form 'scaffolding' is also widely used.

items.definition: To draw answers or ideas out of learners by asking questions or using prompts, instead of simply supplying the information yourself.
items.example: I try to elicit the target language rather than model it, so that my learner is producing, not repeating.
items.note: Rare outside education. Do not confuse with 'illicit'. The noun is 'elicitation'.

items.definition: To show learners how to do something by giving an example of the language, the process or the behaviour to imitate.
items.example: First I model a good answer, then my student records her own version of it.
items.note: In this teaching sense the stress is on the first syllable: MODEL. 'A role model' is a different word.

items.definition: To show clearly by doing or explaining how something works, so that learners can understand the process.
items.example: The instructor demonstrated how to navigate the learning platform before the task began.
items.note: Very common in technical instruction. 'Demonstrate that...' means to prove that something is true.

items.definition: A short final part of a lesson in which the whole class gathers to review what has been covered and to check understanding.
items.example: In the plenary we checked what each group had learnt and set the homework for the week.
items.note: A specialist British education term. American English would say 'a wrap-up' or 'a review'.

items.definition: A short, light activity at the start of a lesson or a training session that gets people talking to each other and relaxed.
items.example: A five-minute icebreaker about weekend plans was enough to get everyone speaking.
items.note: One word, though 'ice-breaker' is also seen. It is used mainly with adults in training.

items.definition: The activity of writing down key information while you listen or read, usually in a shortened and organised form.
items.example: Note-taking in English became much easier once my learner started using headings instead of full sentences.
items.note: The noun is usually written with a hyphen: note-taking.

items.definition: A technique for organising ideas by placing a central topic in the middle and branching related words and images around it.
collocations: a mind map of the unit
items.example: We built a mind map of the unit vocabulary, and she added her own examples in a different colour.
items.note: The verb is usually hyphenated: mind-mapping. 'Mind map' is the common noun in British English.

items.definition: A study method in which you review material at increasing intervals, so that each review comes just before you would forget it.
items.example: She set her flashcards to come back every few days, which is the basic idea behind spaced repetition.
items.note: The key word is spaced. Repeating something several times in one sitting is not the same thing.

items.definition: Judging your own work or your own progress against a standard, rather than relying only on a teacher's judgement.
items.example: The self-assessment at the end of the module made her realise which skills still needed work.
items.note: Hyphenated when it comes before a noun: a self-assessment exercise.

items.definition: To form a clear mental picture of something, or to represent an idea as a diagram, chart or image.
items.example: Try to visualise the room in your home office; it makes the vocabulary much easier to remember.
items.note: British English -ise. The noun is 'visualisation'. The word can also mean to imagine something realistically.

items.definition: A concept that people differ in how they prefer to take in information, for example visually, aurally or by doing something.
items.example: The learning style discussion was interesting, but I reminded her that mixing methods works better for everyone.
items.note: Often used loosely. Research does not support matching teaching to one fixed style.

items.definition: A person who tends to understand and remember information more easily when it is presented as images, diagrams or written text.
items.example: She is a visual learner, so she underlines grammar rules in colour and turns them into small mind maps.
items.note: Use the hyphen when the word comes before a noun: a visual learning style.

items.definition: A person who tends to learn more easily by listening, discussing or repeating material aloud rather than by reading it.
items.example: Because he is an auditory learner, I gave him a recording of the interview to listen to twice.
items.note: 'Aural' is also used, but 'auditory' is the standard term in education.

items.definition: A person who learns best through physical movement, by handling objects or by being actively involved in the task.
items.example: The kinaesthetic learner in my class learns fastest when she has to move around or handle the objects.
items.note: Spelled 'kinaesthetic' in British English; American English uses 'kinesthetic'.

items.definition: A person who prefers to take information in through reading and to produce language in writing.
items.example: For a reading and writing learner, a text-based lesson with follow-up writing seems to work well.
items.note: The slash form is common in course catalogues; 'reading and writing learner' is the plainer version.

items.definition: The total amount of mental effort used in working with and remembering information; when it is too high, learning breaks down.
items.example: Breaking the long text into sections reduced the cognitive load, and my learner finally enjoyed the article.
items.note: A specialist term from educational psychology, but very useful when discussing lesson design.

items.definition: Awareness and control of your own thinking, including judging how well you understand something and planning how to learn it.
items.example: Learning to check her own understanding gave her a metacognitive skill that helped in every other subject.
items.note: Often written with a capital M in academic writing. Many learners find it hard to pronounce.

items.definition: To bring a piece of information back into your mind, either while you are using it or later from memory.
items.example: A short recap at the start of the lesson helps my learner recall the previous week's vocabulary.
items.note: Do not confuse with 'recollect', which is more formal and usually describes memories of events.

items.definition: The ability to keep information in your memory and still be able to use it later.
items.example: Repeated review improved her retention far more than any single memorisation session.
items.note: Usually uncountable in this sense. A 'retention rate' is the percentage reported in education surveys.

items.definition: Actively bringing information out of memory, for example by recalling a definition, rather than simply rereading it.
items.example: We turned the review session into retrieval practice, and she found it harder than she expected but more useful.
items.note: Also called the 'testing effect' in research. The effort of struggling is what strengthens the memory.

items.definition: The act of deliberately prompting your memory for something, which strengthens the memory you have already formed.
items.example: Active recall beats rereading, so I asked her to reconstruct the lesson from memory at the end.
items.note: Related to retrieval practice: the practice is the action, active recall is the effort behind it.

items.definition: The ability to give your full attention to a task, or the particular thing that your attention is directed towards.
items.example: Notifications pulled my learner's focus away, so we agreed to switch them off during study hours.
items.note: The verb takes 'on': focus on. As a noun it is usually uncountable: a lack of focus.

items.definition: The sustained ability to keep your attention on a task without being distracted, especially over a long period.
items.example: Quiet background music improved her concentration during the reading task.
items.note: Usually uncountable. In chemistry 'concentration' means something quite different, so beware in coursebooks.

items.definition: Something that takes your attention away from the task you are supposed to be doing.
items.example: Her phone was the biggest distraction, so she moved it to another room during the hour.
items.note: Countable, usually 'a distraction'. 'Distracted' describes the person, not the thing.

items.definition: Describing a space, an app or a working mode that removes interruptions so that you can concentrate fully.
items.example: A distraction-free app that blocks social media turned out to be the most useful tool she tried.
items.note: It is an adjective and needs a noun after it: a distraction-free environment.

items.definition: The reason or set of reasons that make you want to do something and keep going, especially when the task is difficult.
items.example: Her motivation dropped when she had no contact with her tutor for three weeks.
items.note: Usually uncountable in this sense, although 'motivations' exists for a person's underlying reasons.

items.definition: Motivation that comes from inside you, because the activity itself is interesting or satisfying rather than for any reward.
items.example: She has intrinsic motivation for languages, but she still needs clear goals to keep a weekly routine going.
items.note: The opposite is 'extrinsic motivation', such as money, marks or pressure from an employer.

items.definition: The habit of putting off a task you have decided to do, usually because you find it uncomfortable or boring.
items.example: Procrastination was the real problem, so we built a small daily task she could finish in ten minutes.
items.note: Stress on the second syllable: pro-CRAS-ti-na-tion. It is very common in self-study advice.

items.definition: To study or deal with material systematically, step by step, until you understand it fully.
items.example: I told her to work through one chapter each evening rather than try to read the whole book at once.
items.note: It can also mean to overcome a feeling: work through your fear. The object is the material, not the person.

items.definition: To practise a skill repeatedly and mechanically until it becomes automatic, especially pronunciation or vocabulary.
items.example: We drilled the irregular verbs for ten minutes, and she finally stopped making the same mistake.
items.note: It can sound old-fashioned, and a teacher telling a class to drill may sound critical. 'Practise' sounds more positive.

items.definition: A group of words or pieces of information that you treat as a single unit, so that you remember them together.
items.example: Learning 'I'd like to make an appointment' as one chunk was far easier than learning five separate words.
items.note: Also used as a verb: chunk the material. As an adjective 'chunky' means thick, which can confuse learners.

items.definition: A word, phrase or image that you use to help you remember information, such as an acronym or a short rhyme.
items.example: The mnemonic she invented for irregular past tenses is now on a card above her desk.
items.note: Stress on the second syllable: mni-MON-ic. It is a noun only, with no common verb form.

items.definition: To add short notes, comments or marks to a text in order to explain or record your own thinking about it.
items.example: I asked her to annotate the article with her own questions rather than highlight every unfamiliar word.
items.note: 'Highlight' marks a word you may have met; 'annotate' adds your own commentary.

items.definition: To think carefully about something that has happened or that you have done, in order to learn from it.
items.example: Every month we reflect on what worked and what did not, and adjust the plan for the next month.
items.note: Usually followed by 'on'. The noun is 'reflection', as in a reflection on the course.

items.definition: To record new words and phrases in a dedicated list, with a note, an example sentence and the date you met them.
items.example: She keeps a vocabulary log in a spreadsheet, with one new expression for every lesson.
items.note: Note the pattern: keep a log, write in a log, add something to a log.

items.definition: The ability to speak or write smoothly and easily, with an appropriate speed and little hesitation.
items.example: Her fluency improved quickly once she stopped worrying about making mistakes.
items.note: Usually uncountable. It describes ease of production, not correctness, which is 'accuracy'.

items.definition: The degree to which something is correct and free from errors, especially in the way language is used.
items.example: Our goal this month is accuracy in the present perfect, even if it means speaking more slowly.
items.note: Different from 'fluency': a speaker can be fluent but inaccurate, or accurate but slow.

items.definition: To continue practising a skill beyond the point of competence, so that it stays reliable even under pressure.
items.example: Typists who overlearn a keyboard layout can type accurately without looking at the keys.
items.note: Rare in everyday English. In general use, simply 'practise until it is automatic'.

items.definition: A period in learning when your performance stops improving even though you continue to study.
items.example: She hit a plateau in speaking for weeks, and the fix was changing her routine rather than studying more hours.
items.note: Usually used with 'hit' or 'reach'. The verb 'plateau' also exists but is less common.

items.definition: The pattern of progress over time, showing how quickly a skill is acquired; it is often slow at first and then speeds up.
items.example: The first month is always on the steep part of the learning curve, so progress feels slower than it really is.
items.note: A 'steep learning curve' means learning is difficult at first, not that it is easy.

items.definition: The link between two devices, people or networks that allows information to be passed between them.
items.example: My video lesson froze twice, so she checked her connection before we started.
items.note: Also used for a personal link: she made a connection with the tutor. Say 'internet connection' for the network.

items.definition: The set of keys on a computer or laptop that you use to type letters, numbers and symbols.
items.example: I taught her a keyboard shortcut so she could paste a paragraph without using the mouse.
items.note: Stress is on the first syllable: KEY-board. The second syllable has a silent b.

items.definition: The main page of a website that appears when you open it, usually with links to all the other pages.
items.example: The teacher's homepage has all the lesson links and the recordings in one place.
items.note: One word. 'Home page' also occurs in British English, but the platform style is 'homepage'.

items.definition: Computer software that can carry out tasks which normally need human intelligence, such as recognising speech or writing text.
items.example: She was surprised that the artificial intelligence tool gave grammar feedback almost as fast as a private tutor.
items.note: Usually abbreviated to AI. In education it raises obvious questions about academic honesty.

items.definition: Permission or the ability to reach and use something, such as a file, a website, a course or a shared drive.
items.example: Check that you have access to the recording before the live session begins.
items.note: Stress moves to the second syllable in the verb: to access the file /əˈkses/.

items.definition: To copy a file or a document from your own device to a website, an app or a cloud service.
items.example: She uploaded her assignment at midnight, five minutes before the deadline.
items.note: The opposite is 'download'. Note the stress shift in the verb: UP-load.

items.definition: To remove something such as a file, a message or a word, often permanently and with no easy recovery.
items.example: He deleted the wrong recording and could not get it back because there was no backup.
items.note: In some apps you can undo a delete for a few seconds. On a keyboard the command is often Del.

items.definition: To press a mouse button or tap on a screen in order to choose an option or open something.
items.example: My learner forgot to click 'save', so half of her answers disappeared.
items.note: Transitive use is common: click the button. In careful writing 'click on' is clearer.

items.definition: To start a device or an application so that it begins working, such as a computer, a camera or a light.
items.example: Remember to switch on the microphone before the online lesson begins.
items.note: A phrasal verb: 'switch on the camera' is correct, and 'switch the camera on' is the alternative pattern.

items.definition: To stop a device from working, usually by pressing a button or using an on and off control.
items.example: We agreed to switch off notifications during the lesson so that nothing distracts her.
items.note: 'Turn off' is an equally common alternative. 'Switch off the lights' is very frequent in British English.

items.definition: To enter your username and password so that you can start using a system, a website or an app.
items.example: I could not log in to the classroom platform until my colleague reset my password.
items.note: The verb is two words: log in. The noun is 'log-in' or 'sign-in' with a hyphen.

items.definition: To end your session on a system or website so that nobody else can use it under your name.
collocations: log out at the end of the session
items.example: Always log out of the shared computer in the study room when you finish.
items.note: Note the contrast with 'log in', which is usually followed by 'to' plus a site: log in to the portal.

items.definition: A secret word or combination of characters that you type to prove that you are allowed to use a system.
items.example: She wrote her new password on a card at home because she forgot it the next morning.
items.note: It is one word and is not written with a capital P in ordinary English.

items.definition: A collection of information stored on a computer under one name, such as a document, an image or a video.
items.example: Send me the file as a PDF and I will mark it before the class.
items.note: Unlike the verb 'to file', the noun is normally singular: a file, not a files.

items.definition: A named place on a computer or a cloud service where files are kept in an organised way.
items.example: I create one folder per unit so that my learner can find every recording easily.
items.note: The word is also used for physical folders, so the meaning is usually clear from context.

items.definition: The main screen of a computer and, in modern systems, the area that shows your icons and programs.
items.example: Her desktop was covered with icons, so we tidied it together at the start of the lesson.
items.note: One word. People often say 'the desktop' meaning the physical monitor, which is also correct.

items.definition: A program such as Chrome or Safari that lets you open and read pages on the internet.
items.example: If the site does not work in one browser, try another before you panic.
items.note: It is a piece of software, not the internet itself, although learners often confuse the two.

items.definition: The flat display on a computer, phone or television that shows images and text.
items.example: During screen sharing she could not read my small font, so I increased the size.
items.note: Do not confuse it with 'curtain'. The phrase 'on screen' is normally written as two words.

items.definition: To make two devices or versions of the same data match each other, so that both show identical information.
items.example: The recording was missing until the app finished syncing with the cloud.
items.note: Normally used as a verb. A 'sync meeting' is American usage that British learners rarely hear.

items.definition: Space on remote servers that you can use to keep files and reach them from any device with an internet connection.
items.example: I store all my lesson materials in cloud storage so I can open them on the train.
items.note: Also known as 'the cloud'. British English accepts 'on the cloud', though 'in the cloud' is less common.

items.definition: A wireless connection that gives a device access to the internet without any cable.
items.example: The wifi in the training room was weak, so we used my phone hotspot instead.
items.note: Also written 'Wi-Fi' or 'wi-fi'. The term has no official meaning and was originally a trademark.

items.definition: A delay between an action on your device and the response, often caused by a weak connection or a busy server.
items.example: There was a two-second lag between her voice and the frozen picture on screen.
items.note: Used for audio and video delay. For a generally slow connection, 'a slow connection' is clearer.

items.definition: To stop working or moving suddenly, often because the software is overloaded or the connection is weak.
items.example: Her screen froze twice during the lesson, so we switched to a phone call.
items.note: It is usually intransitive here. 'Freeze up' is very common in informal speech.

items.definition: To stop working completely and unexpectedly, usually because of a software or a hardware fault.
items.example: The app crashed while I was recording, and I lost the first five minutes.
items.note: In formal English say 'the app crashed' rather than 'the app crashed itself'.

items.definition: A second copy of your data that you keep so that you can recover it if the original is lost or damaged.
items.example: Do a backup of your recordings every week; my app lost three lessons last month.
items.note: It can be a noun or a verb, with no hyphen: I back up my files as a verb, in two words.

items.definition: A document made of rows and columns, used to organise, sort and calculate numbers and text.
items.example: She tracks her vocabulary in a spreadsheet with three columns: word, example and date.
items.note: Often called 'Excel' in informal speech, but a spreadsheet is any such program or file.

items.definition: A set of slides used to present information, usually in a presentation or a lecture.
items.example: I asked her to bring a slide deck on her company to class so that we could practise describing data.
items.note: In business English 'deck' is often used on its own, while 'slides' is the more formal word.

items.definition: A video or audio file that captures what was said or shown, and the act of making such a file.
items.example: I made a recording of the lecture so that she could listen again before the test.
items.note: Usually counted: a recording, recordings. The verb is 'record'.

items.definition: A device that captures your voice and sends it to a speaker, a live call or a recording system.
items.example: The browser asked for microphone permission, and she allowed it before we started practising speaking.
items.note: In formal English 'microphone' is one word; 'micro phone' as two words is old-fashioned.

items.definition: A combination of keys that gives you a quick command, or a faster route to something on a screen.
items.example: She learned one keyboard shortcut that saved her a lot of time when she was taking notes.
items.note: Also used figuratively: a shortcut to success. On a keyboard it is written Ctrl + C.

items.definition: A program designed for a particular purpose, especially one you install on a phone, tablet or computer.
items.example: She installed an app that records her pronunciation and compares it with the model answer.
items.note: Short for 'application'. Using 'app' for a desktop program is informal in careful writing.

items.definition: To change something so that it has the newest information or the latest version of the software.
items.example: The app updates itself every month, but she still checks that her notes have synced.
items.note: Noun and verb are both 'update'. As a noun it is normally countable: an update.

items.definition: A message or an alert that appears to tell you about something new, such as an email, a comment or a deadline.
items.example: Turning off notifications on her phone was the first thing we did, and her focus improved that week.
items.note: Usually plural 'notifications'. On a phone they are also called 'alerts'.

items.definition: A screen that shows the most important figures and status at a glance, often in charts or tables.
items.example: The learning dashboard shows her attendance, her scores and her progress against the syllabus.
items.note: Originally a car panel, so it is now used for any overview of key metrics.

items.definition: Software that helps a teacher control a class, for example by locking screens, distributing activities or monitoring progress.
collocations: set up a classroom management tool
items.example: With a classroom management tool I can lock every screen during the exam so that nobody opens a chat window.
items.note: Normally uncountable as a category, but 'a classroom management tool' is natural when you mean one product.
